steps.label: Denary to Hexadecimal: Why Divide by 16?
steps.content:
Denary to Hexadecimal: Why Divide by 16?

Think → Pair → ShareThe left hexadecimal column counts 16s. Predict: how can you find how many 16s are in 75?Show the worked answer

Divide 75 by 16. 16 goes in 4 times (64), with 11 left over. So 75 is 4 sixteens and 11 ones.

  • Hexadecimal columns are 16 and 1.
  • Divide by 16. The whole number is how many 16s: the left digit.
  • The remainder is what is left over: the right digit.
  • Change 10 to 15 into A to F.
  • Check: left digit × 16 + right digit.
75 ÷ 16
75 ÷ 16 = 4 remainder 11
4 sixteens: left digit 4. Remainder 11 = B: right digit.
Place value161
Digit4B
Value411
Worth4 × 16 = 6411 × 1 = 11

4B: 64 + 11 = 75

steps.label: Predict: 90 in Hexadecimal
steps.content:
Predict: 90 in Hexadecimal

Think → Pair → ShareIn 50 ÷ 16 = 3 remainder 2, which number tells you how many 16s, and why?Show the answer

items.explain: The 5 sixteens are the left digit. The remainder 10 is one digit: A. So 5A. Check: 5 x 16 + 10 = 90.

steps.label: Compare: Which Digit Goes First?
steps.content:
Compare: Which Digit Goes First?

Think → Pair → ShareSam converts 75 and writes B4. Why is that wrong, when 4 and 11 are the right numbers?Show the worked answer

B4 means 11 sixteens and 4 ones: 11 × 16 + 4 = 180, not 75. The number of 16s must go on the left.

  • The whole number counts the 16s, so it goes on the left.
  • The remainder goes on the right.
  • Convert back to check. A slip shows up straight away.
Ana: 4B
4 × 16 + 11 = 75
Back to 75: right.
Sam: B4
11 × 16 + 4 = 180
180 is not 75: wrong.

steps.label: Three Digits: Why Divide Again?
steps.content:
Three Digits: Why Divide Again?

Think → Pair → Share500 ÷ 16 = 31 remainder 4. Why can 31 not be the left digit?Show the worked answer

One digit can only hold up to 15. 31 sixteens is too many for one column, so divide 31 by 16 again.

  • Divide by 16. The remainder is the right digit.
  • Whole number more than 15? Divide it by 16 again.
  • That remainder is the middle digit. The new whole number is the left digit.
  • Check with the place values 256, 16, 1.
500 ÷ 16 = 31 remainder 4
Right digit: 4
31 ÷ 16 = 1 remainder 15
Middle digit: F. Left digit: 1

steps.label: Why 4 Bits Make One Hexadecimal Digit
steps.content:
Why 4 Bits Make One Hexadecimal Digit

Think → Pair → ShareOne hexadecimal digit has 16 values. Predict: how many bits do you need to make 16 different patterns?Show the worked answer

4 bits. Each extra bit doubles the patterns: 2, 4, 8, 16. So 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

  • 1 bit: 2 patterns. 2 bits: 4. 3 bits: 8. 4 bits: 16.
  • 16 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 (2 to the power 4).
  • 4 bits go from 0000 to 1111: 0 to 15, just like one hexadecimal digit.
  • A group of 4 bits is called a nibble.
  • 8 bits = 2 nibbles = 2 digits. 12 bits = 3 nibbles = 3 digits.

steps.label: Binary to Hexadecimal: Split Into Nibbles
steps.content:
Binary to Hexadecimal: Split Into Nibbles

Think → Pair → SharePredict: how could you change 10111100 to hexadecimal without working out its denary value?Show the worked answer

Split it into two nibbles, 1011 and 1100. Change each nibble to one digit: B and C.

  • Split the bits into nibbles, starting from the right.
  • Each nibble has place values 8, 4, 2, 1.
  • Add them, then change 10 to 15 into A to F.
  • One nibble gives one digit, even 0000 (the digit 0).
84218421
10111100
BC

1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 = B

1100 = 8 + 4 = 12 = C

So 10111100 is BC

steps.label: Compare: Why Split From the Right?
steps.content:
Compare: Why Split From the Right?

Think → Pair → Share111010 has 6 bits. Why do we split it from the right, and not from the left?Show the worked answer

The right bit is always worth 1. Splitting from the right keeps every bit in its place value. Then fill the last nibble with 0s on the left.

  • The right bit is worth 1, so start there.
  • Not enough bits for the last nibble? Add 0s on the left.
  • Adding 0s on the left does not change the value.
From the right
0011 1010
3A
58, the same as 111010.
Right.
From the left
1110 10
E2
226, but 111010 is 58.
Wrong.

steps.label: Hexadecimal to Binary: One Digit, Four Bits
steps.content:
Hexadecimal to Binary: One Digit, Four Bits

Think → Pair → ShareTo go back from hexadecimal to binary, predict: how many bits does each digit become, and why?Show the worked answer

4 bits each. One digit has 16 values, and 4 bits make exactly 16 patterns.

  • Change each digit to its value (B = 11).
  • Write that value as 4 bits: 8, 4, 2, 1.
  • Put the nibbles side by side, in the same order.
  • Two digits give 8 bits. Three digits give 12 bits.
161
3B

3 = 2 + 1 = 0011. B = 11 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 1011.

84218421
00111011
3B

So 3B is 0011 1011

steps.label: Compare: Why Every Digit Needs 4 Bits
steps.content:
Compare: Why Every Digit Needs 4 Bits

Think → Pair → ShareSam writes the hexadecimal number 81 in binary as 1000 1. Why is that wrong?Show the worked answer

1000 1 is 10001, which is 17. The 1 must be 0001, so 81 is 1000 0001, which is 129.

  • Every digit becomes exactly 4 bits.
  • Small digits need 0s: 1 is 0001, 0 is 0000.
  • Count your bits: 2 digits, 8 bits.
Ana: 4 bits for every digit
1000 0001
= 128 + 1 = 129, the same as 81.
Right.
Sam: 1 written as 1
1000 1
= 10001 = 17, not 129.
Wrong.
